outcome: Nothing in the window has moved the existence question for odd weird numbers: the bounds in force remain no odd weird number below 10^21 (Fang; the 10^21 figure dates from 2014, written up in 2022) and that any odd weird number has at least 6 prime divisors (Liddy and Riedl, 2018). The two in-window items concern a neighbouring question, Erdős problem #825 (the abundancy threshold for distinct-divisor sums): Daniel Larsen's note posted 31 January 2026, and Kei Hisamoto's arXiv preprint of 28 July 2026. Neither says anything about whether an odd weird number exists, and I found no in-window computation, proof, or AI-attributed result on odd weird numbers.
problem_asks: Whether at least one odd weird number exists. Unpacked: (a) a positive odd integer n; (b) n is abundant, meaning σ(n) > 2n, i.e. its proper divisors sum to more than n; (c) n is not semiperfect (pseudoperfect), meaning no subset of n's proper divisors sums to n. The bullet asks only for the existence of one such n. It does not ask for a count, a bound, a classification, or whether odd weird numbers are infinite. The bullet has no parent. Erdős problem #470 pairs this question with the infinitude of primitive weird numbers, but this bullet does not ask that, so events bearing only on primitive weird numbers are recorded as neighbouring rather than as bearing on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Robert A. Hearn, comment on OEIS A006037 (25 May 2005): 'There are no odd weird numbers < 10^17.' A pre-window computational bound. The OEIS comment is the only public statement of it I found, and it was superseded by Fang's later searches.
events.delivers: No odd weird number below 10^17, by a finite search. Nothing beyond that range.
events.remains: The existence question for every odd n at or above 10^17.
events.time_since_posted: about 21 years; superseded by Fang's 2013-2014 searches, which report the same kind of result to a higher bound
events.directly_checkable: A finite search. The OEIS comment does not describe its method or code.
events.direction: Neither way. A finite search finds no odd weird number in its range and cannot show that none exists beyond it.

events.what_happened: Wenjie Fang, comment on OEIS A006037 (4 Sep 2013): 'There are no odd weird numbers < 1.8*10^19.' A pre-window computational bound, superseded by the 2014 comment below.
events.delivers: No odd weird number below 1.8×10^19, by a finite search.
events.remains: The existence question for every odd n at or above 1.8×10^19.
events.time_since_posted: about 13 years; superseded by the 2014 bound
events.directly_checkable: A finite search; method not described in the comment.
events.direction: Neither way. Finite search, no odd weird number found in range.

events.what_happened: Wenjie Fang, comment on OEIS A006037 (23 Feb 2014): 'No odd weird number exists below 10^21.' The comment says the search ran on the volunteer computing project yoyo@home. erdosproblems.com (#470) and the 2022 arXiv write-up (arXiv:2207.12906) both credit this bound to Fang. Pre-window.
events.revisions: Written up as arXiv:2207.12906 (26 Jul 2022), see that event.
events.delivers: No odd weird number below 10^21, by a finite computer search with no abundance restriction (per the OEIS comment and the arXiv abstract). A bound, not a settlement.
events.remains: The existence question for every odd n at or above 10^21.
events.time_since_posted: about 12 years; cited as established by erdosproblems.com, which does not say the computation was checked
events.directly_checkable: A finite search; the algorithm is described in arXiv:2207.12906, and the data repository github.com/fwjmath/ows-data is linked from that paper (not opened).
events.direction: Neither way. Finite search, no odd weird number found below 10^21.

events.what_happened: Wenjie Fang, on the rechenkraft.net 'Odd Weird Search' forum (post by fwjmath, 23 Feb 2015): a batch covering odd numbers below 10^28 with abundance at most 10^14 found no odd weird number. The post reports 4.3×10^12 abundant numbers checked and about 230,000 workunits, and says the null result went against the expectation. A later post (24 Feb 2015) says a paper is 'in preparation'. The OEIS records the result on 25 Feb 2015 as 'No odd weird number with abundance less than 10^14 exists below 10^28'. The write-up appeared as arXiv:2207.12906 in 2022. Pre-window.
events.delivers: A restricted finite search: no odd weird number below 10^28 with abundance σ(n)−2n at most 10^14. It does not cover odd numbers below 10^28 of larger abundance, and says nothing above 10^28.
events.remains: Odd n below 10^28 with abundance above 10^14; all odd n above 10^28; existence in general.
events.time_since_posted: about 11 years; forum replies only asked for the paper (23-24 Feb 2015) or for news (30 Jul 2016)
events.directly_checkable: A finite search with a stated abundance restriction; the batch data are said to be on the project's GitHub (not opened).
events.direction: Neither way. Restricted finite search, no odd weird number found in range.

ai.disclosed_cost: About 230,000 workunits on volunteer computing; the forum estimates 150 years on a single core.

events.what_happened: Wenjie Fang, 'Searching on the boundary of abundance for odd weird numbers', arXiv:2207.12906 (26 Jul 2022), one author. The abstract reports the computations: no odd weird number below 10^21, and no odd weird number below 10^28 with abundance below 10^14. It describes the search as an application of reverse search and gives an implementation in Sections 2 to 4 (section titles seen; PDF body not readable). This is the first public write-up of the 2014 and 2015 computations, and it is recorded as the event because it is the first written argument for the 10^21 bound. Pre-window.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (26 Jul 2022), per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: No odd weird number below 10^21 (full range, per the abstract). No odd weird number below 10^28 with abundance below 10^14 (per the abstract). Both are finite searches.
events.remains: Odd n at or above 10^21 without restriction; odd n above 10^28 or with abundance at least 10^14; existence in general.
events.time_since_posted: about 4 years (Jul 2022 to Oct 2026). I found no independent reimplementation or public check; erdosproblems.com cites it as established without saying it was checked.
events.directly_checkable: A finite computer search with an algorithm described in the paper; code and data at github.com/fwjmath/ows-data (not opened).
events.direction: Neither way. Finite searches, no odd weird number found in range.

events.what_happened: Farid Jokar, 'On k-layered numbers', arXiv:2207.09053 (submitted 19 Jul 2022). Per a search snippet (the PDF body was not readable to me), Conjecture 6.2 states that every odd abundant number is semiperfect, and notes that Fang and Beckert found no odd weird numbers up to 10^21. This conjecture is equivalent to the non-existence of odd weird numbers, so the event is a restatement that points toward the negative answer, not a result.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (19 Jul 2022), per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing established. It poses a conjecture that would answer the question negatively.
events.direction: Conjectures the negative answer: that no odd weird numbers exist, equivalently that every odd abundant number is semiperfect.

events.what_happened: Jacob Liddy, honours thesis 'An algorithm to determine all odd primitive abundant numbers with d prime divisors', University of Akron (2018), with Jeffrey Riedl listed as research sponsor. The abstract says the algorithm was used 'to prove that an odd weird number must have at least 6 prime divisors'. erdosproblems.com (#470) credits the result to 'Liddy and Riedl' [LiRi18]. Pre-window.
events.revisions: The Akron record shows a last revision of 3 May 2023 (record metadata; the content change is not known).
events.delivers: Any odd weird number has at least 6 prime divisors, per the abstract's wording. The thesis PDF was not readable to me, so I cannot say whether 'prime divisors' means distinct primes or counts multiplicity.
events.remains: Whether any odd weird number exists at all; the structure of odd weird numbers with six or more prime divisors.

checked_by.what_they_did: Read and approved the thesis, per the record that lists them as readers. No published verification or re-derivation found.

events.directly_checkable: The result is a finite enumeration by an algorithm; the thesis PDF (366 KB, link on the record page) describes it, and I could not read it.
events.direction: Restrictive rather than a resolution. It says any odd weird number would have at least 6 prime divisors. It neither produces nor excludes one.

events.what_happened: Gianluca Amato, Maximilian Hasler, Giuseppe Melfi and Maurizio Parton: 'Primitive abundant and weird numbers with many prime factors', arXiv:1802.07178 (Feb 2018; Journal of Number Theory 201 (2019), per the arXiv record snippet), and 'Primitive weird numbers having more than three distinct prime factors', arXiv:1803.00324 (Mar 2018; Rivista di Matematica dell'Università di Parma 7(1), 2016). They build primitive weird numbers with up to 16 prime factors (largest 14712 digits) and say the techniques could be used to search for odd primitive weird numbers. They do not decide the odd question. Neighbouring: about primitive weird numbers, not odd weird numbers. Pre-window. Read from search snippets; the arXiv pages were not opened.
events.revisions: arXiv:1802.07178 published in J. Number Theory 2019 (per snippet); arXiv:1803.00324 journal reference Parma 2016 (per snippet).
events.delivers: Explicit primitive weird numbers with up to 16 prime factors, and counts of primitive abundant numbers by prime-factor count (per snippets). Not statements about odd weird numbers. Per the 2019 abstract summary: all primitive weird numbers with an odd prime factor of multiplicity above 1 and Ω = 7 are found, and none with Ω < 7. These are about a restricted class of primitive weird numbers and do not settle existence.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks: existence of an odd weird number, and any count or bound for odd weird numbers.

checked_by.who: Journal of Number Theory (referees not named in what I read), for arXiv:1802.07178
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for computational number theory
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication in 2019 (per the journal reference in the arXiv record snippet)
checked_by.where: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.07178 (not opened; journal reference seen in search snippet)

events.direction: Neither way on odd weird existence. Constructions and enumerations for a neighbouring class (primitive weird numbers).
events.object: Explicit primitive weird numbers with up to 16 prime factors, the largest with 14712 digits. These are even or odd-factored weird numbers of a different class, not odd weird numbers, so they bear on nothing in this bullet.

events.what_happened: Giuseppe Melfi, 'On some questions about weird numbers', talk at the Third Italian Number Theory Meeting, CRM Pisa (22 Sep 2015), and a paper 'On the conditional infiniteness of primitive weird numbers' (venue not confirmed; erdosproblems.com cites it as [Me15]). The talk abstract says all known weird numbers are even, the odd question is open, and recent computations exclude odd weird numbers up to 10^21. Pre-window. Read from search snippets; the CRM page was not opened.
events.delivers: Infinitely many primitive weird numbers, conditional on a prime-gap bound (p(n+1) − p(n) < (1/10)·p(n)^(1/2) for large n), which the erdosproblems.com page says follows from well-known prime-gap conjectures such as Cramér's. It is about primitive weird numbers, not odd ones. The talk restates the odd question as open.
events.time_since_posted: about 11 years; cited on erdosproblems.com, with no assessment of the argument found
events.direction: Neither way on odd existence. Conditional result on a neighbouring question (primitive weird numbers).

events.what_happened: Imane Sahel, MSc thesis 'On some Quadratic Diophantine Equations and Semiperfect Numbers', American University of Sharjah, submitted April 2025 (advisors Abdel Rahman Yousef and Issam Louhichi). Per the repository record (read from a search snippet), it counts solutions of χ^α + y² = z², treats abundant, semiperfect and primitive weird numbers in a second part, and draws observations on odd and even perfect numbers. The PDF is embargoed until 15 Sep 2026 and I could not read it, so whether it says anything about odd weird numbers is unknown.
events.delivers: Not established by what I could read. The metadata does not state any result on the existence of odd weird numbers.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, as far as I could establish.

checked_by.what_they_did: Named as supervisors. Their approval of the thesis is implied by the record's acceptance but not confirmed.

events.time_since_posted: about 18 months; no public engagement found
events.direction: Unknown. Not established what, if anything, it says about odd weird numbers.

events.what_happened: On erdosproblems.com (forum thread 825, 31 Jan 2026, first post 03:28), user DanielLarsen posted a note hosted at github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-825/blob/main/825.pdf, saying it 'is a note which I believe resolves this problem'. The #825 page now marks the problem 'solved in the affirmative by Larsen'. The displayed statement is: for any ε > 0 there is L such that if every prime divisor of n exceeds L and σ(n) > (2+ε)n, then n is the distinct sum of proper divisors of n. The #825 question is Benkoski–Erdős's: is there an absolute constant C with σ(n) > Cn implying n is a distinct sum of its proper divisors. The erdosproblems.com #470 page links to #825 for the remark that if there are no odd weird numbers, every weird number has abundancy index below 4. The note itself was not readable to me.
events.revisions: Forum posts 31 Jan to 1 Feb 2026 (16 comments in total). The #825 page's last edit is 1 Feb 2026. No version history of the PDF is visible.
events.delivers: On #825, as displayed: for n whose prime divisors all exceed L(ε) and σ(n) > (2+ε)n, n is a distinct sum of proper divisors. This covers only n with large prime divisors; the full #825 question quantifies over every n with σ(n) > Cn. As a constraint, it implies that any weird n with σ(n) > (2+ε)n has a prime divisor at most L(ε). It says nothing about whether an odd weird number exists.
events.remains: Odd weird existence entirely. On #825, whether the full quantifier ('every n with σ(n) > Cn') is covered depends on what the note proves, which I could not read; the page's 'solved' label rests on the displayed restricted statement.

checked_by.who: Thomas Bloom, maintainer of erdosproblems.com; his unit-fractions density result is the basis of the approach the forum describes
checked_by.qualification: Subject expert and the site's maintainer
checked_by.what_they_did: Replied 'Very nice!' on 31 Jan 2026, said the argument likely also answers Erdős's question about divisors below εn, and suggested stronger versions. In the posts I read he did not state that he had checked the argument.

events.time_since_posted: about 8 months (31 Jan 2026 to 11 Oct 2026). No verification or error report found. The thread's posting has been suspended.
events.directly_checkable: The note itself (GitHub PDF). A formalisation was started by a forum user (Kevin Barreto) with no result posted; the posts name Aristotle as a tool to try.
events.doubts: The displayed statement covers only n with all prime divisors above L(ε) and abundancy above 2+ε, while the question quantifies over all n. Whether the note closes the question as posed depends on its content, which I could not read.
events.direction: Affirmative on #825 in the restricted form displayed. No direction on odd weird existence.
people: Daniel Larsen (forum handle 'DanielLarsen'; identity with the Wikipedia article's Daniel Larsen not confirmed)

events.what_happened: Kei Hisamoto, 'On weird numbers with high abundancy index', arXiv:2607.25278 (v1, 28 Jul 2026). Theorem 1.1, per the HTML text: if the abundancy index of a natural number n exceeds 633, then n is semiperfect (a sum of distinct proper divisors). Remark 2 attributes to Desmond Weisenberg the observation that a weird number with abundancy index above 4 has an odd weird divisor, and quotes Erdős's question 'Are there any odd weird numbers?'. The paper does not mention Larsen. The problem it addresses is the #825 question.
events.revisions: v1 only (28 Jul 2026), per the arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: On #825: C = 633 works for every natural number n, per Theorem 1.1, with no restriction on prime divisors. This is wider in scope than Larsen's displayed restricted statement. On odd weird numbers: nothing. It neither decides existence nor adds any constraint beyond the Weisenberg remark, which is cited, not proved.
events.remains: Whether any odd weird number exists (entirely). Whether 633 is near the sharp constant for #825, which the paper does not settle as far as I read.
events.time_since_posted: about 11 weeks; no public comment found
events.direction: Affirmative on the #825 question: a constant exists (C = 633), for all n. Says nothing about parity.

disputes.summary: Erdős #825 is marked 'solved in the affirmative' (Larsen, forum, 31 Jan 2026), but the displayed statement covers only n whose prime divisors all exceed L(ε) and whose abundancy exceeds 2+ε. Hisamoto (28 Jul 2026) claims C = 633 for every n. Which of these, if either, closes the #825 question as posed is for the judging pass. Neither bears on odd weird existence, which is the only question this bullet asks.
The erdosproblems.com #470 page credits 'Liddy and Riedl' with the 6-prime-divisor result. The thesis record lists Jacob Liddy as author and Jeffrey Riedl as research sponsor, not co-author.

The 10^21 search is credited to 'Fang' by erdosproblems.com and by arXiv:2207.12906, which has one author. A search snippet of arXiv:2207.09053 (Jokar) credits 'Fang and Beckert' with the same search. I could not read the body of 2207.09053 to check the citation.

The #825 solver appears as forum user 'DanielLarsen', and the GitHub repository is under 'Larsen-Daniel'. The Wikipedia article on Daniel Larsen describes an MIT undergraduate who proved Carmichael-number results and does not mention Erdős problems. I could not confirm the two are the same person.

summary: The question is the bullet's one existence question: does an odd weird number exist. Its state is that it is open, and the bounds are as old as the record. The computational bound is no odd weird number below 10^21. Fang first announced this in OEIS comments in February 2014, after earlier bounds by Hearn (10^17, 2005) and Fang (1.8×10^19, Sep 2013), and wrote it up as arXiv:2207.12906 on 26 July 2022 (one author; the abstract is the only part I read, since the PDF was not readable). Fang also reported, in a forum post of 23 February 2015 and in the write-up, a restricted search below 10^28 for odd numbers with abundance at most 10^14: 4.3×10^12 abundant numbers and about 230,000 workunits, with no hit; the forum said a paper was in preparation, and the arXiv paper is the only write-up I found. The structural bound is that any odd weird number has at least 6 prime divisors, from Liddy's 2018 Akron honours thesis (the abstract is read; the thesis PDF returned 403 to my fetch). None of these is in the window. In the window, I found two events, both on the neighbouring question Erdős #825 rather than on odd numbers. The first is a forum note by DanielLarsen posted 31 January 2026 (GitHub PDF, not readable to me), which the #825 page now marks as solving the question. The page's displayed statement covers only n whose prime divisors all exceed L(ε) and whose abundancy exceeds 2+ε, while the question ranges over all n. The forum shows praise from Thomas Bloom but no stated verification, and no error reports. The second is Kei Hisamoto's arXiv:2607.25278 (28 July 2026), whose Theorem 1.1 (read from the HTML text) gives C = 633 for all n with abundancy above 633; it cites Weisenberg's remark that a weird number with abundancy above 4 has an odd weird divisor, and quotes Erdős's odd-weird question, but it says nothing about parity or the existence of odd weird numbers. The Erdős #470 page, Wikipedia's Weird number article, and OEIS A006037 (both last edited 9 Sep 2026) all still describe odd weird existence as open with the same bounds, and the 2026 Tao AI-contributions wiki (frozen 30 Jun 2026) has no entry for #470, #825, or weird numbers. Close calls: (i) whether the Larsen note, if sound, counts as settling #825 is a scope question for the judging pass, and is not this bullet; (ii) the #470 page's 'solved' label rests on a restricted statement; (iii) Hisamoto's 633 bound, if correct, answers #825 for every n, which would make the Larsen statement look like a special case rather than the resolution. AI: no system is credited with any mathematics in any event. Fang's and Liddy's work was computational or algebraic and predates the AI period. The 825 thread names Aristotle (Harmonic's prover) as a tool to try for autoformalisation, and Kevin Barreto says he started a formalisation run 'with my system' (unnamed). That is peripheral and produced no result, so none_found is false for the Larsen event with systems empty. The Hisamoto preprint has no AI mention and no acknowledgements section. For the AI search, I searched for AI and odd weird numbers together, for AlphaEvolve, GPT-5, and Erdős AI databases, and for AI-attributed results on #470 and #825, and found nothing that credits a system with odd weird mathematics. The Tomodovodoo profile linked from #470 mentions work with Harmonic's sponsorship on other problems; I found no link between that and #470. Dead ends: the 2024 Integers paper, a journal version of arXiv:2207.12906, a Fang publication under other titles, and a Larsen arXiv posting were not found. Several sources were read only from search snippets and are marked opened false.
competing_reading: The strongest case for treating the Fang line as a moved bound: the bullet asks about odd weird numbers, the bound 10^21 is the quantity a reader cares about (how large a counterexample must be), and the 2022 arXiv write-up is a dated public argument. Against that, every step is before the window, so it moves nothing since 26 January 2024. In-window, the strongest case for counting the Larsen note as relevant: the #470 page links #825 as a remark about odd weird numbers, and if the note is sound the page would call #825 settled, so a reader could infer something about weird numbers' abundancy. The record does not support that inference for parity. A weird n with abundancy above 2+ε has a prime divisor at most L(ε), which constrains a hypothetical odd weird number but does not show one exists or not. Finally, the strongest case that the Hisamoto preprint matters here is weak: its 633 bound is a statement about the abundancy of all weird numbers and so bounds the size of any odd weird one's abundancy only through the Weisenberg remark, which is quoted, not proved.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Larsen PDF: its title, author, date, the exact theorem (how L depends on ε and whether n is restricted to large primes), and any statement about tools; and confirmation whether the forum user is the same person as the Wikipedia article's Daniel Larsen. (2) The full text of the Liddy thesis: whether 'prime divisors' means distinct primes, and any acknowledgements. (3) The body of arXiv:2207.12906 and the data at github.com/fwjmath/ows-data, to check the search statements and any tool disclosure, and whether any batch after 2015 extended the 10^21 or 10^28 bounds. (4) The body of arXiv:2607.25278, checked against the proof and any later citation. (5) The body of arXiv:2207.09053 to check Conjecture 6.2 and the 'Fang and Beckert' attribution. (6) For any claim of an odd weird number, the explicit object and its check; none has been reported in the window.
